html:
Updated to the new 2026 slides (Dr. Rafif Mattar — sent Nov 2026). Black = her slides, and "Slide notes" = the speaker notes written under her slides (from Principles and Practice of Surgery, 8th ed., the reference on her last slide). Green = Dr. Abobotain's notes from the earlier version of this lecture — still valid. Lines marked (2025 slide) were on the old deck only. Red = every past-exam fact.

1. Introduction

  • Preoperative assessment is fundamental to achieve good surgical outcomes.
  • Consider if the patient is medically fit to undergo the proposed procedure.
  • The benefits of the surgery outweigh the potential risks.
  • May take place in a dedicated assessment clinic a few weeks before surgery.
  • Allows the patient to be admitted to hospital on the day prior or on the actual day of surgery.

Slide notes: the surgeon should consider whether the patient is medically fit enough to undergo the proposed procedure and whether the benefits outweigh the potential risks and severity of any complications. Assessment culminates in admission on the preceding day or, more usually, on the actual day of surgery.

Pre-operative medicine — a multidisciplinary team

  • Multidisciplinary team: anaesthesia and surgery · other medical specialties.

Slide notes: coordination of expertise from a multidisciplinary team including doctors from other specialties such as anaesthesia and surgery, and medical specialties.

Pre-operative assessment = pre-procedure assessment. It is not limited to surgery: it applies to any invasive procedure (e.g. GI endoscopy, interventional radiology / endovascular procedures).

Goals: give the best possible treatment, minimize preventable complications/errors, and decide whether the procedure is appropriate and safe.

  • Who needs an extensive pre-op assessment? The patient with significant uncontrolled disease, e.g. 60-year-old with atrial fibrillation + uncontrolled CHF — not the healthy young patient or the patient having a skin excision under local. 442
  • Day-surgery open hernia repair → the service you need pre-operatively is Anesthesia. 437 ×3

2. The preoperative assessment pathway

Slide notes: good-quality assessment and appropriate optimisation before admission mean many patients can be admitted on the day of surgery. Thorough assessment = detailed medical history, systematic enquiry, physical examination, then laboratory, radiological and other investigations as directed by the history, examination findings and the nature of the surgery.

3. Classification of surgery (Table 7.1)

Slide notes: it is helpful to classify surgery by magnitude, e.g. the system proposed by NICE.

Surgery gradeExamples
MinorExcising skin lesion · draining breast abscess
IntermediatePrimary repair of inguinal hernia · excising varicose veins in the leg · tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy · knee arthroscopy
Major or complexTotal abdominal hysterectomy · endoscopic resection of prostate · lumbar discectomy · thyroidectomy · total joint replacement · lung operations · colonic resection · liver resection · radical neck dissection

4. Risk assessment — ASA physical status (Table 7.2)

Slide notes: patients having surgery are classified according to the American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) score.

ASASlide descriptionDoctor's description (Dr. Abobotain)
ASA 1A normal healthy patientNo systemic disease — uncommon before disease-related surgery, more likely in elective/cosmetic procedures
ASA 2A patient with mild systemic diseaseMild systemic disease without significant functional limitation
ASA 3A patient with severe systemic diseaseSevere systemic disease with functional limitation, but not a constant/immediate threat to life
ASA 4Severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to lifee.g. end-stage liver failure or severe heart failure awaiting transplant
ASA 5Moribund patient, not expected to survive 24 hours with or without surgerye.g. severe trauma with life-threatening head injury or active intra-abdominal haemorrhage
ASA 6Patient with brainstem death undergoing organ retrievalBrain-dead organ donor
  • In the event of an emergency procedure, "E" is placed after the Roman numeral.
  • After confirming the indication and completing history, examination and investigations, decide the risk of operating on this patient. Being a surgical candidate only means the patient can have surgery — the decision still depends on whether surgery is necessary, benefit > risk, and whether risk can be reduced.
  • ASA reflects systemic disease severity and threat to life, not surgical complexity.
  • Smoker with well-controlled hypertension, no end-organ damage → ASA II. 442 ×2
  • Well-controlled asthmatic having an emergency appendectomy → ASA 2E (add "E" for emergency). 431
  • Obese (BMI 32) day-surgery patient assessed as low–intermediate risk → the reason is the BMI (obesity 30–40 = ASA II). 436
2025 slide — ASA classification (old deck) (1)

5. Preoperative assessment by system

  • CVS · Respiratory · Medications & allergies · Pregnancy.
Slide icons — heart, lungs, medications, pregnancy (4)

History & physical (2025 slide)

  • First step in any pre-op assessment.
  • Must include past medical & surgical histories.
  • Verify indications for surgery.
  • Rule out contraindications for surgery.
  • Review recent investigations and order others if needed.
  • First & crucial step: establish the presenting problem/diagnosis, past medical history, past surgical/anesthetic history, and current functional/medical status.
  • Comorbidities may need optimization before elective surgery — e.g. a patient needing cholecystectomy with uncontrolled diabetes: control glucose first, then operate; operating with severe hyperglycemia increases complications.
  • Why prior anesthetic history matters: previous surgery/anesthesia may reveal preventable risks — prior anaphylaxis to an anesthetic/medication, or previous surgical/anesthetic complications. Identify these beforehand to prevent recurrence.
  • Family history of malignant hyperthermia → avoid the triggers: depolarizing muscle relaxants (succinylcholine) AND volatile anesthetic agents (use TIVA); dantrolene is the treatment, not the prevention. 442

Verify the indication (doctor)

  • Does the patient actually need surgery? What is the indication?
  • Are there non-operative/alternative treatments? Are there any contraindications?
  • Key principle: being technically able to operate ≠ the operation is necessary or best. Some patients can undergo surgery but should not, because risk/benefit favours another option.
  • Review all previous investigations (MRI, CT, etc.) personally and add further investigations if needed — do not rely solely on another clinician's conclusion.

Cardiovascular system

Slide notes: assess the severity of cardiovascular disease and look for signs of undiagnosed or inadequately treated disease. History: exercise tolerance, existing cardiovascular disease or risk factors (e.g. hypertension) and symptoms (chest pain, intermittent claudication, syncope). Angina or previous MI may indicate significant coronary artery disease; patients may have had PCI (angioplasty, stenting) or cardiac surgery (valve surgery, bypass grafting).

Slide notes: exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea → left ventricular failure; significant dependent oedema → right-sided heart failure. Blackouts and dizzy spells → arrhythmias, valvular heart disease or cerebrovascular disease. Examination should detect arrhythmias, murmurs, hypertension and signs of cardiac failure. New or worsening symptoms should be assessed before surgery; antiplatelets/anticoagulants may need to be stopped or modified. Formal assessment (e.g. cardiopulmonary exercise testing) in certain groups.

Cardiac assessment (2025 slide)

  • ECG ± echo, stress testing, blood tests (e.g. creatinine level).
  • Assess perioperative MI risk.
  • Risk factors such as age, smoking, CHF, lung and kidney disease.
  • Optimize cardiac function pre-op, modify risk factors.
  • Assess cardiac status even when overt cardiac disease is not known — occult disease/arrhythmias may become significant under anesthesia. Get at least an ECG, particularly when risk factors are present; further tests depend on findings/risk.
  • Perioperative MI risk: surgery = physiologic stress → ↑ cortisol + catecholamines → ↑ cardiac workload → MI, which may occur hours or even a day after a technically successful operation.
  • Major risk factors: age (non-modifiable), smoking (modifiable), heart failure/CVD, lung disease, kidney disease, diabetes and other comorbidities.
  • High-risk cardiac patients may need cardiology assessment/optimization; if surgery can safely wait, optimize cardiac function first.

Respiratory system

Slide notes: new or increased cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheeze may indicate undiagnosed respiratory disease or an exacerbation. In asthma, COPD or fibrotic lung disease, purulent sputum = infective exacerbation. In asthmatics, previous ICU/hospital admissions and steroid dependency = severe disease. Functional respiratory reserve is best assessed by exercise tolerance (how far on the flat, up an incline, how many stairs before resting). Significant dyspnoea → pulmonary function tests.

Slide notes: patients with an acute respiratory illness should have surgery postponed where possible — increased risk of bronchospasm and post-operative bacterial pneumonia; general anaesthesia makes it worse by depressing ciliary function.

  • Active wheezing in the holding area before an elective hernia repair → postpone surgery (key in 438 and 436; one 436 version keyed "local anesthesia + avoid airway manipulation" — marked "not sure" by the compilers). 438 436 436
  • Severe COPD (SpO₂ 88%) before abdominal surgery → the most effective way to prevent post-op respiratory failure is effective pain control + incentive spirometry. 442

6. Medications

  • Long-term steroid therapy.
  • Antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulants.
  • Oral contraceptives and hormone-replacement therapy.
  • Psychiatric drugs.
  • Diabetes.
Drug groupSlide notes
Long-term steroidsMay cause hypoadrenalism → cannot mount a response to surgical stress → an increased dose is usually needed (amount depends on the procedure). Signs of hypoadrenalism: hypotension/shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia — look for them in any unwell steroid-dependent patient post-op; urgent steroids may be needed to avoid an Addisonian crisis
Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel)Withdrawal risks thromboembolic events, particularly MI. Do not withdraw before stent endothelialisation — takes up to 6 months. Weigh against surgical bleeding; if feasible, postpone surgery and withdraw only after consulting a cardiologist or vascular surgeon
Anticoagulants (warfarin, NOACs)Balance thromboembolic risk of stopping vs bleeding risk; NOACs need special peri-operative consideration; use of bridging anticoagulation
OCP / HRTDepending on surgery and other VTE risk factors, it may be advisable to stop oestrogen-containing drugs 4–6 weeks beforehand — balanced against the risk of unwanted pregnancy
SSRIsSerotonin syndrome with tramadol; ↑ bleeding with NSAIDs or warfarin
LithiumNarrow therapeutic index, renally excreted (accumulates in renal dysfunction), interacts with anaesthetic agents and muscle relaxants; arrhythmias, GI upset
TricyclicsNeed not be stopped, but alert the anaesthetist (hypotension, arrhythmia)
MAOIsInteract with opiates and vasopressors; ideally stop 2–3 weeks before surgery; in an emergency avoid opiates and pressor agents

Medication assessment (2025 slide)

  • Discontinue ASA/anticoagulants ahead of time.
  • Surgery-specific meds may need to be stopped (e.g. AEDs).
  • Continue BP, DM and other meds even when NPO.
  • Always obtain a complete medication history, especially anticoagulants/antiplatelets: aspirin, warfarin, DOACs/NOACs. Surgery may sometimes proceed while on them, but the team must know beforehand — each agent has its own pre- and post-op interruption window.
  • Procedure-specific adjustment — e.g. epilepsy surgery needing intra-op EEG localization: antiepileptics may be withheld because they blunt EEG activity and hide the focus.
  • BP and diabetes medications are generally continued even when NPO, depending on the plan.
  • Warfarin: stop 5 days before surgery and bridge with LMWH (high thrombotic risk, e.g. AF). Older keys say "1 week" — same idea: stop it ahead, don't continue it and don't give vitamin K for elective surgery. 442 441 437 436 ×2
  • Therapeutic LMWH: stop 24 hours before surgery. 442
  • Drug-eluting stent → delay elective non-cardiac surgery ~6 months (on DAPT) — matches the slide notes (endothelialisation takes up to 6 months); older keys: ~1 year and stop clopidogrel 5–7 days before. Never operate early or stop DAPT early for elective surgery. 442 441
  • Drugs to continue: statin and beta-blocker (ACEI/ARB are often held the morning of surgery; warfarin is stopped). 441
  • CKD patient with bleeding risk → DDAVP (desmopressin) pre-op (uremic platelet dysfunction). 437
  • Hypothyroid patient for elective lap chole → reschedule until euthyroid (risk of myxedema coma after surgery in hypothyroid patients). 438 ×2 438

Steroid cover (from past exams)

SituationWhat to do
Short course in the past (e.g. prednisone 3 days, 2 months ago)No extra supplementation [q:31f039b4439]
On steroids + minor surgery (e.g. inguinal hernia, prednisolone 10 mg)Continue usual dose, no supplement [q:20796e43441]
On steroids + moderate surgery (e.g. total knee replacement)Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction, then 25 mg q8h for 24 h [q:369ef4db437 ×2]
On steroids + major surgery (e.g. thoracic)Usual morning dose + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg q8h [q:28208477442]

Diabetes

  • Glucose + HbA1c matter because diabetes is common and strongly affects perioperative risk. Poor control → infection, metabolic/acidosis complications, diabetic emergencies/coma. Elective surgery may need delay until diabetes is adequately controlled.
  • HbA1c 14 before elective cosmetic breast reduction → agree with the surgeon who refused: uncontrolled diabetes = high risk (ASA 3); optimize first. 436
  • Insulin: hold rapid-acting insulin from midnight before surgery (when NPO). 437
  • Tight glucose control decreases the incidence of deep wound infection. 438

7. Allergies

  • Medications, foods.
  • Common examples: antibiotics · chlorhexidine · adhesive dressings · latex.

Slide notes: for patients with severe latex allergy the environment must be cleared of latex (gloves, rubber bungs on drug vials, other surgical and anaesthetic equipment). Latex allergy is decreasing, while allergy to chlorhexidine is rising.

  • Penicillin-allergic patient for AAA repair with a synthetic graft → clindamycin (or vancomycin). 437

8. Pregnancy

  • Elective surgery should be avoided in pregnancy.
  • If necessary, it is best in the 2nd trimester.
Table 7.3 — Peri-operative risks of surgery in pregnant patients
Spontaneous abortion or premature labour (highlighted on the slide)
Hypotension in the supine position — IVC compression in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters (highlighted)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux — increased risk of aspiration
Hypoxia — high metabolic rate and reduced functional residual capacity
Teratogenic effects of drugs — particularly in the 1st trimester (highlighted)
Pre-eclampsia / eclampsia
Amniotic fluid embolism
  • Pregnancy: the second trimester is the safest time for (non-urgent) surgery. 437
  • Pregnancy: the safest time to operate is the second trimester (1st = organogenesis/miscarriage risk, 3rd = preterm labour and the gravid uterus gets in the way). 439 Final ×2

9. Investigations — patient vs surgery risk

  • Blood tests: CBC · coagulation · U/E · cross-matching.
  • ECG · CXR · others.
Slide icons — blood test, ECG, CXR, others (4)

Slide notes: for many patients in good health undergoing relatively minor surgery, preoperative investigations are not required. With more severe comorbidities or major surgery → FBC, coagulation screen, U&E, ECG or respiratory function tests may be needed. Women of child-bearing age should be asked if they might be pregnant and a pregnancy test done. A family history of sickle cell disease/trait may require testing. Self-reported poor exercise tolerance correlates with increased perioperative risk.

  • A completely healthy 20-year-old for inguinal hernia repair needs no investigations. 439
  • Who needs a pre-op ECG? The older patient — e.g. 60-year-old for elective lap cholecystectomy (not the 22-year-old for breast implants). 441

Pre-op testing (2025 slide)

  • General blood tests (e.g. PTT/INR, CBC, Chem, HCG).
  • Specific blood tests (e.g. LFTs, tumor markers, hormonal profiles).
  • Imaging (e.g. X-rays, CT, MRI, etc.).
  • Type & screen / crossmatch.
  • Glucose and HbA1c for diabetic patients.
2025 slide — sample pre-operative testing grid (old deck) (1)
TestPurpose / notes (doctor)
CBCEnsure adequate Hb/blood counts — undiagnosed anemia matters, especially before procedures with expected significant blood loss
Coagulation profile (INR/PTT)Identify anticoagulation/coagulopathy even before apparently minor procedures — a missed abnormality can cause major bleeding even in a "small" procedure
Chemistry / electrolytesIdentify electrolyte/metabolic abnormalities
Pregnancy testIn patients of childbearing potential when appropriate — affects anesthesia and urgency; ask whether the procedure can safely wait
  • Coagulation — do not assume "minor": check coagulation broadly rather than assuming a small procedure is harmless. Rare severe maternal situations may require pregnancy termination to save the mother.
  • Procedure/disease-specific tests: order what is relevant — e.g. liver surgery → liver function assessment.
  • Tumor markers may be diagnostic, prognostic, or a baseline for post-op surveillance:
    • Prostate cancer → PSA: baseline before treatment; post-resection decline = response; a later rise may mean recurrence.
    • Pituitary tumors → hormonal assessment: diagnosis/classification, may decide treatment, useful for follow-up.
    • Example — prolactinoma: pituitary mass + high prolactin → usually medical treatment rather than surgery; serial prolactin levels monitor response/recurrence.
  • Imaging: obtain imaging appropriate to the anatomy/pathology being treated — e.g. fracture/joint replacement → X-ray ± further imaging; depending on the condition → CT, MRI, MRCP, specialized imaging.
  • Blood availability — rule of thumb: have appropriate type and screen ± cross-match. Not every procedure needs cross-matched blood, but unexpected vascular injury/major bleeding can happen even during apparently minor procedures — have at least type and screen ready before any intervention where bleeding could become significant.

10. Pre-hab

  • Undergoing a major surgical procedure is associated with significant physiologic stress.
  • Increasing functional capacity prior to surgery is associated with better outcomes.
  • Particular relevance to older patients.
  • Targets: physical activity · smoking · nutritional status · obesity · alcohol.

Pre-hab

Slide notes: functional improvement may be associated with fewer postoperative complications and shorter hospital stay; specific respiratory-muscle training reduces postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs). Smoking cessation benefits can be seen with just 4–6 weeks of cessation. Nutrition: low BMI, ≥ 20% weight loss, hypoproteinaemia and hypoalbuminaemia are all associated with more complications, including delayed anastomotic and wound healing. Obesity: increased risk from surgery and anaesthesia. Alcohol: acute vs chronic alcoholism.

Smoking

  • Heavy smokers may benefit from delaying elective surgery — the professor gave ~6 weeks of smoking cessation as an example. Smoking ↑ MI, stroke, surgical-site infection, poor wound healing, wound dehiscence.
  • Stop smoking 4–6 weeks before surgery — the best way to prevent post-op pulmonary complications in a smoker (6 weeks before lung surgery). 442 441 441 437
  • Elective plastic surgery: the history item that affects the surgical result is smoking (poor flap/wound healing). 437 Final

Nutrition & obesity

  • Low albumin = marker of nutritional deficiency before surgery. 430 ×2
  • Marked weight loss from lower esophageal carcinoma: the keys disagree — 431 keyed central parenteral nutrition, 428/429 keyed gastrostomy ("the patient can still use his GI tract"). Principle: if the gut works, use it (enteral); a gastrostomy is avoided when the stomach will be the conduit for esophagectomy. 431 ×2 429 ×2
  • Obese patients have more complications partly because procedures take longer. 438

11. VTE prophylaxis

  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) accounts for thousands of deaths each year due to fatal PE.
  • Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) may also cause morbidity.
  • Prevention of VTE is therefore cost-effective.

DVT and pulmonary embolism

Slide notes: many VTE deaths are hospital-acquired; DVT also causes chronic problems (leg ulcers, decreased mobility).

  • All surgical patients are assessed for: thrombosis risk and bleeding risk.
Slide icons — thrombosis vs bleeding (3)
Table 7.10 — risk of THROMBOSISTable 7.11 — risk of BLEEDING
Patient: advancing age · obesity (BMI > 30) · previous VTE · family history of VTEPatient: active bleeding · uncontrolled hypertension
Medications: HRT · oestrogen-containing contraceptivesMedications: anticoagulants · antiplatelet agents
Clinical: malignancy · dehydration · thrombophilias · pregnancy or within 6 weeks post-partumClinical: inherited or acquired bleeding disorders · thrombocytopenia
Procedural: immobility · lower-limb or pelvic surgery · surgery > 90 minutes · admission to critical careProcedural: spinal, ophthalmic or neurosurgery · spinal/epidural anaesthetic · lumbar puncture

Tables 7.10 (thrombosis) and 7.11 (bleeding)

Mechanical vs medical (Table 7.12)

MechanicalPharmacologic
Antiembolism stockings (knee- or thigh-length)Low-molecular-weight heparin
Foot impulse devicesUnfractionated heparin
Intermittent pneumatic compression devices (knee- or thigh-length)Fondaparinux

Slide notes: continue thromboprophylaxis until mobility is no longer significantly reduced — usually 5–7 days, except orthopaedic lower-limb surgery: 2–4 weeks after surgery.

12. Antibiotic prophylaxis

  • The use of antibiotics perioperatively to reduce the incidence of surgical site infection (SSI).
  • The risk of SSI depends on patient and operative risk factors, including the wound class.
WoundExamplesSSI with prophylaxisSSI without
CleanThyroidectomy, breast surgery, CABG, knee replacement, uncomplicated hernia repair1–2%1–2% — no role for prophylaxis unless an implant/mesh is used
Clean-contaminatedElective cholecystectomy, elective appendectomy, urinary stone removal (no UTI), LSCS, laparoscopic hysterectomy, prepared bowel surgery~3%6–9%
ContaminatedEmergency cholecystectomy, emergency appendectomy, bowel opened in obstruction, major asepsis break (e.g. open cardiac massage)~6%~20%
DirtyAbscess drainage, peritonitis, faecal contamination, neglected traumatic wound > 6 h7–8%20–40%

Slide notes: SSI accounts for ~16% of hospital-acquired infections; every surgical patient should be assessed for SSI risk. A single IV dose is often adequate if its half-life covers the operation; repeat the dose if surgery lasts > 4 hours.

  • Uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy → peri-operative ceftriaxone + metronidazole (no 72-hour course). 439
  • Elective splenectomy: give the vaccines against encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae) 2–3 weeks before the operation (emergency splenectomy → ~2 weeks after). 437 Final ×2

Infection prevention (2025 slide)

  • Pre-op glycemic control.
  • Nutritional status.
  • Immunocompetence assessment.
  • Pre-incision antibiotics, repeat intra-op dosing.
  • Adequate sterilization.
  • Optimize risk factors: glycemic control (uncontrolled DM ↑ infection), hypertension/vascular disease, significant systemic disease, malnutrition/emaciation, morbid obesity.
  • Assess immune competence: poorly controlled DM, comorbidities, primary immune deficiency, acquired immunodeficiency/immunosuppression.
  • Give pre-incision prophylactic antibiotics when indicated; re-dose ~every 4 hours during prolonged surgery.
  • Sterilization: clean OR, properly sterilized instruments; degree of contamination depends on the procedure.
SpecialtyConsideration (doctor)
NeurosurgeryGenerally clean, except infected sites or entry through colonized mucosa (transnasal/transoral) — infection → meningitis, potentially fatal
OrthopedicsDeep infection → osteomyelitis, may be severe enough to need amputation
Bowel / some ENTMore exposure to normal flora — less inherently clean
  • Universal rule: sterility standards depend on the field, but correct OR/instrument sterilization is essential in all cases.

13. Preoperative fasting

  • To ensure an empty stomach and minimise the risk of regurgitation and aspiration during induction of anaesthesia.
  • Extended periods of fasting are usually not required.
  • Where possible, patients should be NPO of food for 6 hours and clear fluids for 2 hours.

Slide notes: avoiding prolonged fasting is an important component of ERAS pathways.

  • Recommended NPO: 6–8 hours (solids). 441
  • Infant on formula milk → 6 hours fasting before GA. 431

14. Emergency surgery

  • Principles of assessment for elective surgery apply equally to the emergency setting.
  • May be reduced by lack of time and information.
  • Emergency patients often require resuscitation prior to surgery.
  • ABC should be the first priority.
  • Emergency (ruptured ectopic) in a diabetic with glucose 13 mmol/L → operate without further investigation; don't delay a life-threatening emergency for ECG/CXR/consults. 430

15. Informed consent

  • Consent to treatment is the principle that a person must give permission before they receive any medical examination, test or treatment.
  • Key components of consent: it must be the patient's decision · all the information they "need to know" must be freely provided · the patient must be able to understand and apply the information · for consent to be valid it must be voluntary and informed, and the person consenting must have the capacity to make the decision.
  • The process: education & provision of information → time to consider, decide & ask questions → consent signed → surgery. The process should start with education and information, delivered in various modalities.
  • Avoid medical jargon. Consider the patient's primary language. It is important that the patient's understanding is confirmed.
  • Often in the first conversation there is information overload — only a small proportion of the information provided is retained.

Slide notes: non-English speakers should be provided an interpreter; for complex elective procedures it is useful to test the patient's understanding.

7 key elements of a surgery consent form
1. Patient identification and procedure details
2. Explanation of risks and complications
3. Information about anaesthesia
4. Alternatives and consequences of non-treatment
5. Right to refuse or withdraw consent
6. Consent to blood transfusion (if applicable)
7. Signature and date

Informed consent (2025 slide)

  • A process by which a patient is informed of: their medical condition · treatment options with descriptions and advantages and disadvantages of each · any possible complications · expected outcome.
  • Patients agree or refuse a specific treatment.
  • Competence and ability to make decisions are crucial, otherwise a surrogate decision-maker is required.
  • Implied consent in certain situations.
  • Extremely important. Inform about: diagnosis, all treatment options, no treatment/observation as a legitimate option, the proposed procedure, possible complications, and expected outcome. A competent patient may refuse treatment even when the condition is treatable — respect it.
  • Discuss all relevant complications, including rare ones, so unexpected outcomes are not completely unknown beforehand.
  • Expected outcome / managing expectations — e.g. decompressive craniotomy after severe stroke may save life but not reverse paralysis; spine surgery does not mean immediate walking. Expected outcome may change whether the patient accepts surgery.
  • Informed consent includes the name of the responsible surgeon (plus diagnosis, procedure, complications, prognosis, other options; the patient can change his mind at any time). 435

Capacity

  • The patient must understand the information and decide. Patients who may lack capacity: confused, reduced consciousness, young children, severe dementia/Alzheimer.
  • If capacity is uncertain: explain, then ask the patient to repeat back what he understood.
  • No capacity → identify an appropriate surrogate (family member, spouse, or other legally/ethically accepted surrogate).
  • A competent 55-year-old whose son came to sign for him → the patient himself must sign. 437 ×2

Implied consent in emergencies

  • Emergency treatment proceeds when the incapacitated patient cannot consent, no surrogate is available, and clinicians reasonably believe the patient would want life-saving treatment.
  • Example: previously healthy 19-year-old with severe head trauma, unconscious and dying, nobody available → treat.
  • Harder when prior wishes/comorbidities make the preference uncertain (e.g. elderly patient with advanced metastatic cancer). Implied-consent decisions commonly need agreement by two physicians that the patient would most likely consent.
  • Life-threatening emergency with no family available → operate; no consent needed (implied consent). 442 441 438 ×2

Patient safety checks (from past exams)

  • Sign in (before induction) = confirm patient identity, site & procedure, consent, and that the site is marked. 435 437
  • Wrong knee listed and site not yet marked → time-out / verification with the team and the patient, then mark the correct site. 442

16. Disease-specific assessment (2025 slide)

  • Patient candidacy for treatment.
  • Required pre-op testing.
  • Availability of required resources.
  • Alternative options.
  • Decide whether the patient is a candidate for this particular treatment, not merely whether they can tolerate surgery — many diseases have several valid treatment modalities.
  • Example — brain metastasis: surgery, radiation, or systemic therapy; choose the option best for this patient. Make sure all required pre-op testing is complete.
  • Do not proceed without resources: essential equipment/devices, personnel/expertise, neurophysiology monitoring or another specialty service. If unavailable, refer/transfer to a center that has them.
  • Alternatives: always consider and discuss them; explain all reasonable options and which is best — the final choice belongs to the informed patient.
  • Metabolic (stress) response to surgery is reduced by a laparoscopic approach (less tissue trauma); longer operations and prolonged fasting make it worse. 438 Final

Liver disease — Child-Pugh (from past exams)

  • Child-Pugh uses albumin, total bilirubin, INR/PT, ascites, encephalopathy (not platelets). 436 ×2
  • Child-Pugh A → anticipated surgical mortality < 10% (B ≈ 30%, C ≈ 80%). 437
  • Final version: Child-Pugh A cirrhosis with sigmoid cancer → mortality if operated < 10%. 437 Final

Mastery checklist (Dr. Abobotain's notes)

  • Optimize modifiable comorbidities (e.g. uncontrolled diabetes) before elective surgery rather than operating through them.
  • Being technically able to operate ≠ surgery is indicated — always verify the indication and consider alternatives.
  • Check coagulation broadly, even before "minor" procedures.
  • Have at least a type and screen ready before any procedure where bleeding could become significant.
  • ASA reflects systemic disease severity and life threat, not surgical complexity — know I–VI (VI = brain-dead donor).
  • Perioperative MI comes from surgical stress (↑ cortisol/catecholamines) and can present hours to a day after an uneventful operation.
  • Anticoagulants/antiplatelets have agent-specific interruption windows.
  • Do not proceed without essential resources — refer instead.
  • Consent covers diagnosis, all options (including no treatment), procedure, complications, realistic outcome.
  • Capacity uncertain → ask the patient to repeat back.
  • Implied consent typically needs two physicians' agreement.
  • Re-dose prophylactic antibiotics ~every 4 hours in prolonged surgery.

Pre-operative Assessment

History and Physical Examination:
  • Obtain patient history with mnemonic “OPQRST”:
  • O: Onset (gradual vs sudden)
  • P: Precipitant (food or movement)
  • Q: Quality (Sharp, dull, cramps)
  • R: Radiation (Back)
  • S: Stop (what offers relief)
  • T: Temporal (Duration)
  • The presence of fever, sweats, or chills usually indicates acute infection, whereas weight loss indicates a chronic condition like tumors.
  • Past medical Hx should include:
  • Prior operations
  • Prior VTE (DVT + PE)
  • Bleeding diatheses
  • Airway problems (anesthesia problems)
  • Active medications
  • Steroid use in the last 6 months (risk of adrenal insufficiency post- operatively)
  • Allergies (egg allergy leading to insecurity with propofol use and iodine use with shellfish allergy)
  • Social Hx should include alcohol, smoking, and illicit drug use
  • Family Hx should include problems related to the patient’s presentation
  • Example: colorectal cancer to test for familial conditions
  • Also check for coagulation, bleeding, and anesthesia problems
  • Example: death of a young patient in the OR might indicate an endocrine problem like pheochromocytoma
  • Also, check for systemic review
  • Obtain patient vital signs along with height, weight, and BMI
Pre-op Testing:
  • Generally, children uncommonly require preoperative lab tests for most operations. On the other hand, a complete blood count, chemistries, and electrocardiogram are proper for higher-risk patients before complex operations
  • A coagulation profile is warranted in most procedures. Conditions include:
  • Brain, spine, and neck surgeries
  • Bile duct obstruction, malnutrition, and absent terminal ileum (Vit K)
  • Pregnancy test for women of childbearing age (Beta-HCG), and blood preparation for transfusion
  • Check patient blood sugar levels as they are correlated with surgical site infections (SSIs)
  • Screen for staph aureus through nasal swabs to guide the decontamination process. MRSA screening is indicated in:
  • Immunocompromised patients
  • Open cardiac surgeries
  • Foreign bodies implantation in orthopedics and neurosurgery
  • Electrocardiograms are indicated in:
  • Older than 50
  • Vascular operations
  • Hx of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, severe pulmonary disease, or renal dysfunction
  • Chest radiographs are indicated in suspicion of malignancy or pulmonary disease
  • Carotid US is indicated in:
  • Carotid bruits
  • Hx of cerebrovascular accident
  • Hx of transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)
  • Non-invasive venous studies are indicated in patients with prolonged immobility and/or hospital stay prior to surgery
Pre-op Process:

1- Risk Assessment and Reduction

  • Essentially based on the ASA score
  • The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) has the following factors for cardiac complications:
  • Hx of ischemic heart disease
  • Congestive heart failure
  • Cerebrovascular disease
  • High-risk operation
  • Pre-op treatment with insulin
  • Pre-op Creatinine of > 2 mg/dl
  • Additional risk factors include:
  • Old age
  • Smoking
  • Insulin-dependent diabetes
  • Coronary artery disease
  • Abnormal cardiac stress test
  • long-term beta-blocker therapy
  • COPD
  • creatinine of > or equal to 1.8 mg/dl
  • Noninvasive stress testing before noncardiac operations is indicated in:
  • Patients with active cardiac conditions (unstable angina, recent MI, significant arrhythmias, or severe valve disease)
  • Patients who require vascular operations and have clinical risk factors and poor functional capacity
  • coronary revascularization before non-cardiac operations is indicated in:
  • Significant left main coronary artery stenosis
  • Stable angina with three-vessel disease
  • Stable angina with two-vessel disease and significant LAD coronary artery stenosis with either an ejection fraction < 50% or ischemia on noninvasive testing
  • High-risk unstable angina
  • Non-ST-segment elevation Ml
  • Acute ST-elevation MI
  • Beta-blockers should be continued among those patients who are already taking them and among those having a vascular operation and at high cardiac risk, including known coronary heart disease or the presence of ischemia preoperative testing
  • Preoperative aspirin usage should continue among patients at moderate to high risk for coronary artery disease unless the risk of resultant bleeding outweighs the likelihood of an atherothrombotic event
  • Thienopyridines, such as ticlopidine or clopidogrel, are administered in concert with aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy following the placement of coronary artery stents
  • Elective operations with a significant risk of bleeding should be delayed 12 months before the discontinuation of the thienopyridine in the presence of a drug-eluting stent, at least 4-6 weeks for bare-metal stents, and 4 weeks after balloon angioplasty
  • Postoperative pulmonary complications (PCCs) have risk factors:
  • Old age
  • High ASA score
  • Congestive heart failure
  • COPD
  • Altered mental status, alcohol, and malnutrition
  • OSA (use STOP-BANG questionnaire to screen)
  • It is recommended to stop smoking at least 4 weeks before surgery (4-6 weeks is acceptable)
  • Pulmonary function tests and baseline arterial blood gas tests guide the care of selected patients, especially those anticipating lung resection. In addition, asthma should be medically controlled
  • The efficacy of stockings for VTE prevention is unproven. This can violate skin integrity and result in the accumulation of edema. A 4-week course of LMWH is recommended, especially in abdominal or pelvic malignancies
  • An extended duration of outpatient prophylaxis with enoxaparin after operations for cancer resulted in a statistically significant reduction in VTE events, compared with inpatient administration only, with no increase in bleeding complications. Therefore, prophylaxis should be maintained after the discharge of patients who have elevated risk scores
  • The relative risk of an SSI seems to increase incrementally in a linear pattern with the degree of hyperglycemia with glucose levels > 140 mg/dl
  • Glucose levels of 181-300 mg/dl prompt the need to begin an infusion of IV insulin before the operation, along with a 5% dextrose solution to minimize the chances of hypoglycemia
  • Patients with glucose levels of > 300 mg/dL are assessed for ketones or acidosis prior to starting an insulin infusion
  • Intravenous insulin is best for perioperative glucose control due to its rapid onset of action, short half-life, and Immediate availability
  • Antibiotics should be administered 1 hour before incision. Additional doses are administered after two-half lives during the operation (4 hours for cefazolin)
  • 1st generation cephalosporins are preferred (Clindamycin if penicillin- allergic)
  • 2nd generation cephalosporins to cover gram -ve and anaerobes (could give 1st generation + metronidazole)
  • When antibiotics are administered for SSI prophylaxis rather than for treatment of an established or suspected infection, they are typically not continued after surgery, except in special circumstances such as vascular grafts, cardiac surgery, or joint replacements
  • The maintenance of perioperative normothermia also has salutary effects on wound oxygen tension levels and can consequently reduce the incidence of SSIs
  • Some data support hyperoxygenation with FiO2 >= 80% during the first 2 hours after a major colorectal surgery. In addition, protocols with mupirocin nasal ointment application and chlorhexidine soap showers have reduced the incidence of SSIs among patients colonized with methicillin- sensitive S aureus
Fluid Management and Blood Volume:
  • Pulmonary artery catheterization is associated with increased mortality rates. It may be considered in selected cases who show clinical cardiac instability with comorbid conditions
  • Dialysis should be performed within about 24-36 hours before an operation to avoid electrolyte disturbances after conferring with a nephrologist
  • Blood transfusions are indicated in cases of blood diatheses after conferring with a hematologist. Since these were found to be associated with high mortality rates, it’s crucial to weigh the benefits and risks
Nutrition:
  • Hypo-albuminemia (albumin < 3.0 mg/dl) is an independent risk factor for the development of SSIs, with a fivefold increased incidence compared to a normal patient.
  • The obesity surgery mortality score for gastric bypass (poor prognosis):
  • BMI >= 50
  • Male sex
  • Hypertension
  • PE risks (Past Hx, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension)
  • Age >= 45
Endocrine:
  • Steroid use should not be done indiscriminately as this increases the risk of infections
  • Thyrotoxicosis should be corrected to avoid thyroid storm:
    • Antithyroid medications (propylthiouracil or methimazole)
    • Beta-blockers and corticosteroids
    • Saturated solution of potassium iodide
  • Hypothyroidism can progress to hypothermia and hemodynamic collapse, so treat with:
    • Hormone replacement (Levothyroxine)
  • CT with contrast should be avoided with goiter patients as this may exacerbate the condition (iodine contrast)
Illicit drugs and alcohol:
  • In general, patients should refrain from illicit drugs for at least 2 weeks before the surgery. They should also refrain from alcohol at least 1 week before the surgery
  • Give benzodiazepines to control the withdrawal symptoms
Cancer Therapy:
  • It is recommended to have at least 4-6 weeks between bevacizumab and an operation, and therapy should not resume until after 4 weeks when the wound heals
Informed Consent:
  • A process by which the patient is informed of their medical condition, treatment options, possible complications, and expected outcomes
  • Patient capacity should be taken into consideration with making decisions. A health proxy should be sorted in case the patient is incapacitated
Preoperative Instructions:
  • Refraining from food/drinks before anesthesia:
    • Liquids: 2 hours
    • Breast milk for infants: 4 hours
    • Formula milk for infants: 6 hours
    • Light meals: 6 hours
    • Fatty meals: 8 hours
  • Patient medications are generally continued until the morning of the surgery. Chronic narcotics, for example, are continued on the day of surgery to avoid withdrawal symptoms
  • NSAIDs, herbal preparations, and vitamin E can disrupt normal coagulation and should be stopped 1 week before an operation
  • Estrogen receptor antagonist (Tamoxifen) should be stopped 2-4 weeks before an operation
  • Stopping Warfarin 5 days before surgery results in the normalization of the INR, and the surgeon will decide if a bridge therapy is required or not
  • DOACs should be stopped 48 hours before the scheduled procedure
Operating room:
  • Local clippers are used to remove hair in the OR. Razors should be avoided due to the risk of infection
  • The addition of isopropyl alcohol to chlorhexidine provides the best outcome in skin preparations
